first_paragraph: Earlier this month I found a one-click universal XSS issue with uBlock Origin (the MV2 Firefox version, although a similar but less problematic issue also affected the MV3 version, uBO Lite), where a malicious website could trick the extension into adding arbitrary trusted filters. Trusted filters can inject JavaScript code into pages, and so the malicious website could create a trusted filter on another website and run arbitrary JS in the context of any site. This issue is fixed now; you can read the GitHub advisory for some more details.GPT-5.6 Sol did most of the hard work of finding the issue. I figured there might be some kind of UXSS from filter injection, so I asked it to take a look, and it found the issue. I then checked and verified the issue it proposed. I wrote all of the prose in this post myself; Claude wrote most of the code for the PoC.uBlock Origin has an element picker that you can pull up by right-clicking on the page. title: Old Bitly links are being hijacked (ransomnews.com)
comments: Link shorteners that are outsourced are in my humble opinion an order of magnitude worse for the internet than they would be if in-house.The way they accrete URLs over time, and then time passes, and anything can happen (your account gets deactivated, shortener company goes out of business / experiences catastrophic data loss / etc) is just asking for permanently broken links which may be unfixable.Especially when you consider how these services can, unless they're spammy enough to inject gross interstitial ad pages, make 0 revenue from you if you aren't currently paying for a premium service, it's easy to see how they can go under.Note: Clearly with the kind of ephemeral crap these 2011 tweets were, I'm assuming the 'attacker' publicized "Hey guys look at these funny tweets" because obviously who cares about 15 year old McDonalds marketing messages. But in general it's sad to see these still being used. To be fair to bitly, they do offer the ability to use your own domain at least, but sadly, with a service targeted mainly at marketing departments, usually they don't have the ability to work with the in-house tech team(s) to even set up DNS.reply

Yeah, but the alternative is everyone having a short domain, which is unfortunately difficult due to the fundamental mathematical principle that a low amount of characters has a very small number of options available.Everything with finite space is expensive, the more finite the more expensive.So, while I am in favour of what you say, and I’m in favour of self-governance as much as possible, I understand the challenges.reply

>Yeah, but the alternative is everyone having a short domain, which is unfortunately difficult due to the fundamental mathematical principle that a low amount of characters has a very small number of options available.I get where you're coming from but I'm wondering if that's undersells the value-add of link shorteners as literally just shortening the link.I remember that I liked using link shorteners because they gave me analytics on who clicked my link and where from. I believe paid QR Code link shorteners operate on a similar principle of offering analytics on where and how QR Codes are discovered.And while in theory, this should be handled by first-party analytics, the users of link shorteners don't necessarily always have control over that analytics platform (e.g., student researchers driving traffic to a survey on an institutional domain).reply

Yes, they existed, but were they really that popular before that use?reply
> moving the goalposts is extremely prevalent on HN<https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=23117242>reply
> mass market… was the original goalpost.Nobody claimed they didn’t exist at all before Twitter.reply

> mass market was the original goalpostGee, thanks.  Maybe insert some more superfluous facts and observations here, like the atomic number of carbon or maybe the price of tea in China."Mass market" is not another way of saying popular.  Even if that were the question—whether TinyURL et al were popular before Twitter came along—the answer is a resounding yes.The claim that "the original mass market use of link shorteners was to minimize the number of characters needed to link from a Tweet" is simply not true.reply

title: Tor Project Issues Rapid-Response DoS-Defense Fix Amid Sustained DDoS Attack (torproject.org)
comments: I started running a non-exit node a few months ago and after a little while it became trusted and became a guard node. Guard nodes seems more important than amiddle node so I was happy to run one I know is legitimate. That makes at least one legitimate guard node for the network.I noticed the attack when my mom said the wi-fi wasn't working well and I checked it out and the download speed was down 99% from normal. And eventually after various other troubleshooting attempts I turned off my mini pc where the relay and other self-hosted services run and the internet speed returned to normal. Yeah I'm not a  very adept sys-admin, AI set up all the docker compose stacks for me.I then looked at my relay on the relay search and it said overloaded. So I checked the Tor forum and sure enough others were reporting the same thing.So at first I tried just lowering the bandwidth let through, although I'd thought it should already not be letting that much through. That did not work.So I made it not become a guard node and now it works fine. But I also read something about malicious guards and exits being how Tor users have been compromised before. So it seems important guards are trustworthy.I'm not gonna risk running a guard again (letting my node become a guard) at least for a while until this attack stabilizes.reply

Over three hours, members of the crowd took turns at the microphone telling harrowing stories about their plights with cancer. The witnesses talked about the fear that gripped them when they discovered they were ill. But then they described how their desperation turned to hope when they learned of a new option for treatment: a chemical compound extracted from apricot pits and bitter almonds. It was known as laetrile.“Four weeks ago, my doctor gave me a clean bill of health,” one man said. “If these people here have had cancer and they were cured—and I’m one of them—then my goodness sakes,” he asked, “why not let the people in this great state use this substance?”The people who testified that day had gone to Mexico for laetrile treatments, because it wasn’t approved for cancer therapy in the United States. You’re right - looking at the scope pictures, the horizontal period of the grid is 2ms, and the period of the wave is just over that.A 240Hz wave would have a period of 4.17ms. 480Hz is 2.08ms. Much closer to the oscilloscope waveforms. And even then the waveforms are periodic, with smaller troughs at every second dip.I wish I could see their test setup. It would be ironic if the panel was fully DC dimmed and the troughs were from another light source or something…I’m not sure why the scope is saying 240 though. It makes me doubt my understanding :-/.[Edit: Ah - got it! It’s measuring the frequency of the very lowest points - the ‘every second dip’]reply

> [Edit: Ah - got it! It’s measuring the frequency of the very lowest points - the ‘every second dip’]

So that's the danger of [the authors] just reading the number off the screen without understanding what the scope is showing.To measure frequency, typically the scope will measure the max and min of a waveform, then select a point halfway between them as the trigger point, then measure the time between successive triggers.  Also, the trigger usually has an intentional hysteresis, so that noise near the midpoint does not cause multiple triggers on a slowly-rising waveform.The little dips don't go down far enough below the midpoint to activate the hysteresis window, which is why it only counts every second dip.Edit to add:  Also, while it's nice that they show all the waveforms with the same vertical scale, they really need to adjust the vertical attenuation for the 0% and 25% brightness steps if they want to measure frequency by reading a number off the screen.  Auto measurements won't work in these cases, when the waveform fills less than half a vertical division.And the waveform trigger is also set incorrectly (0V, with DC coupling on the input...) because none of the waveforms have a rising edge on the center graticule line, where the trigger annunciator is.reply
Just adding a note to future readers: frequency is correctly measured dip to dip or top to top. Or every second time a particular value is reached.reply

> Or every second time a particular value is reached.The value is waving, so a complete cycle is when it got back to where it started: that is, not just its value but its _direction of change_ is also the same.(A value waving in 3D could coincide with its start value multiple times before it completes a whole cycle.)reply

The difficulty here is that it's 480Hz top-to-top, but there are two definitions of dip-to-dip depending on if you count every 'dip' from 100% (480Hz), or just the ones that reach the lowest voltage ⃰ (240Hz).⃰  ⃰(brightness - presumably the test setup is an LDR or something?)reply

And that the actual display modulates at 240Hz but that some portions of the screen are 180 degrees out of phase with other portions.  Or that one of the subpixel colors is out of phase with the others.  This could explain the weird alternating-depth signal at ~2ms intervals.Here's notebookcheck's review methodology:https://www.notebookcheck.net/How-does-Notebookcheck-test-la...And the sensor they use might be this one:https://www.thorlabs.com/item/PDA100A2That doesn't look like it's even close to being able to focus on a single subpixel or even a single row without additional optics.In any case, the 0% and 25% waveforms look pretty bad.  In my experience, light with sharp, short pulses (like "driverless" LED lights produce) are unpleasant, but the unpleasantness is related to how bright the source is compared to everything else in the field of view.  (The 0% and 25% waveforms are solidly at twice the frequency of driverless LEDs, which will make the effect considerably less bad.)reply
